objective: Measure platform initiatives with DORA metrics: deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate and time to restore, and how a platform moves them
secondaryObjectives: Platform efficiency and team productivity: adoption, time to first deploy, support load, cost per workload and developer satisfaction surveys

sources.cite: CNCF Certified Cloud Native Platform Engineering Associate (CNPA) curriculum: Platform Engineering Core Fundamentals 36%, Platform Observability, Security and Conformance 20%, Continuous Delivery and Platform Engineering 16%, Platform APIs and Provisioning Infrastructure 12%, IDPs and Developer Experience 8%, Measuring your Platform 8%
sources.note: On 2026-11-17 the weights were confirmed through a third-party study page (kube-dojo.github.io/k8s/cnpa, summarizing fetch), which lists 'GitOps fundamentals' and continuous delivery in the core fundamentals domain and says to 'understand why GitOps uses pull-based reconciliation'. The official curriculum was not re-read; the objective wording is the course seed's. Reused for REQ-336 from this course's service-selector-no-endpoints-cnpa (the same reading and date); the objective wording is the course seed's.

Read 2026-11-17 with WebFetch (a summarizing fetch) of the primary page, found by WebSearch. Confirms: throughput (change lead time, deployment frequency, failed deployment recovery time, which replaced time to restore) and instability (change fail rate, deployment rework rate), applied per application or service; the aim is a team improving on itself, not competing with other teams, and broad targets invite gaming (Goodhart's law).

sources.cite: CNCF TAG App Delivery, Platform Engineering Maturity Model
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 with WebFetch (a summarizing fetch) of the primary page, found by WebSearch. Confirms: platform measurement through standardized surveys and feedback channels, adoption and time saved, and lead time and build times; at higher maturity a platform is run as a product with product management, user research and shared roadmaps.

The company, the platform, the tenant teams and the people are fictional. The minutes or days each step takes and the effects of each decision are teaching simplifications for exam practice, not measured values.

brief.situation: You lead the internal developer platform at Halberd Insurance, a fictional insurer. The CFO wants to know whether the platform's budget is paying off. You have three weekly reviews to agree how the platform will be measured.
handover: Data available: pipeline runs and deploy events, change tickets, incident records, platform support tickets, and an annual survey.
A proposal from finance: rank developers by commits and tickets closed.
howItWorks: The board shows the risk register against the appetite, each stakeholder's support in words and the docket.
Move on a week at a time. A decision comes to you at each platform review; before the first, you can read the evidence.
At the end you write the record and a short reflection.

then.log: Week 2: commit counts double as people split changes; incidents rise 30% and nothing about delivery improved.

whichPrompt.title: What to measure
whichPrompt.context: Finance proposes commits and tickets closed per developer.

choices.label: Use the DORA delivery metrics per team (deployment frequency, change lead time, change fail rate, and failed deployment recovery time, DORA's current name for time to restore), from pipeline and incident data, with the pre-platform baseline

effects.log: The four keys are agreed, per team, with a baseline.

choices.feedback: The four keys balance speed (frequency, lead time) against stability (failure rate, restore time).

choices.label: Report deployment frequency only: it is the easiest to show
choices.feedback: Speed without stability can be gamed by shipping smaller broken changes.

choices.label: Accept finance's commits and tickets per developer

effects.log: Commits and tickets per developer are adopted.

choices.feedback: Activity counts reward splitting work and closing tickets, not delivering safely.

usePrompt.title: A league table?
usePrompt.context: The VP asks for a ranking of teams and individuals in the monthly all-hands.

choices.label: Show each team its own trend and the platform's effect, use them in team retrospectives, and never rank individuals
choices.feedback: DORA metrics guide a team's improvement; ranking turns them into targets that get gamed.

choices.label: Rank teams, not individuals, at the all-hands
choices.feedback: Less harmful, but teams with harder systems look worst and start optimizing the number.

choices.label: Rank individuals and tie it to reviews
choices.feedback: When a measure becomes a target for people's reviews, it stops measuring anything.

dxPrompt.title: Mandate or measure?
dxPrompt.context: Six teams still deploy outside the platform. Support tickets about the platform doubled last quarter.

choices.label: Track adoption, time to first deploy, support load and a short quarterly satisfaction survey; interview the six teams and fix what keeps them off
choices.feedback: A platform is a product: adoption earned by solving users' problems, measured with their feedback.

choices.label: Track adoption only
choices.feedback: You see who uses it, not why the six don't, or how painful it is.

choices.label: Mandate the platform for everyone by next month; no survey
choices.feedback: Forced adoption without fixing the pain points pushes teams to workarounds.

reflection.question: Write the measurement decision for the CFO: what the platform will be measured on, how the numbers will be used, and what it shows so far.

scoring.modelReasoning: DORA's keys measure software delivery outcomes (DORA's current model calls time to restore failed deployment recovery time and adds deployment rework rate): deployment frequency and lead time for speed, change failure rate and time to restore for stability, per team and against a baseline. They guide improvement; ranking teams or people makes them targets and corrupts them. A platform is a product: its own measures are adoption, time to first deploy, support load and developer satisfaction, and adoption is earned rather than mandated.
